item.content:encoded:
With the recent release of plans to build on top of Eero Saarinen's terminal building at Dulles International Airport, we take a look at old and new controversies surrounding significant works of architecture and their preservation across the US.

Preserving historic architecture is no easy task given ageing buildings, lack of funding and the lucrative nature of new development.

From a Tadao Ando beach house gutted by musician Kanye West, to Frank Lloyd Wright's only realised skyscraper and Donald Trump's many renovation projects around Washington DC, the legal battles below showcase the often bitter fights that ensue over preserving architecture

Some of the projects have been completely renovated and refreshed, while others are scheduled for demolition, but most are suspended between the two – and have been for years.

Read on below for 11 contentious architectural preservation battles across the US.

The White House East Wing, Washington DC

The East Wing of the White House was demolished in October 2025 to make room for a giant ballroom promoted by president Donald Trump.

Preservationists pushed back on the plans, with various judges issuing injunctions to stop the building, despite approval of the new designs by local regulatory bodies. As of July 2026, construction will reportedly include an expansive underground security complex.

Questions about the legality of the demolition and construction are still being worked out in the courts.

Find out more about the White House East Wing ›

The Vaillancourt Fountain, California, by Armand Vaillancourt

This peculiar fountain in San Francisco was ruled a hazard in November 2025 by the San Francisco Arts Commission, which voted to dismantle it in anticipation of renovations to the surrounding plaza.

Despite the outcry from locals, the city began to take down the fountain earlier this year, but not before it briefly caught fire due to debris catching flame from a construction blow torch.

Find out more about the Vaillancourt Fountain ›

Dallas City Hall, Texas, by IM Pei

Late last year, the Dallas city government voted to explore relocating operations from its 1970s brutalist city hall building designed by architect IM Pei, where it currently resides, citing the building's age and cost of maintenance. A move would cast the future of the iconic structure in uncertainty.

The debate to remain in the building or relocate has sparked much local debate, with reports stating that the voting council is starkly divided.

Find out more about the Dallas City Hall ›

550 Madison skyscraper, New York, by Philip Johnson and John Burgee

After the iconic New York skyscraper sat vacant, architecture studio Snøhetta proposed a renovation that would see parts of the structure clad in glass.

The initial scheme proposed a multi-storey glass block to replace the tower's base, but after the building was granted landmark status shortly, Snøhetta pared back the design and conserved the entirety of the facade.

The studio completed the toned-down renovation in 2022.

Find out more about 550 Madison skyscraper ›

Miami Marine Stadium, Florida, by Hilario Candela 

An ongoing preservation saga has plagued Miami Marine Stadium since its closure in 1992. Since then, it has remained vacant and graffitied on its unique site where it sprawls out over a local harbour.

Conservation group Docomomo selected it as one of the most under-threat buildings in America in 2022, and Miami locals will vote to approve an operator for the stadium in the hopes of conserving it during primary elections in August, according to the Miami Herald.

Find out more about Miami Marine Stadium ›

Portland Municipal Services Building, Oregon, by Michael Graves

Michael Graves' 1982 Portland Municipal Services Building in Portland was one of the first buildings in the US to kickstart the preservation of postmodern architecture.

In 2014, the building came under threat of demolition, but with the help of advocates, including from Graves himself, Portland city council eventually decided on an extensive renovation and the building reopened in 2020.

Find out more about Portland Municipal Services Building ›

Price Tower, Oklahoma, by Frank Lloyd Wright

In late 2024, Frank Lloyd Wright's only skyscraper underwent a contentious legal battle between a local owner and The Frank Lloyd Wright Conservancy, when the latter discovered the "unapproved" sale of original furniture from the interior.

Litigation was recently settled in March 2026 after a new owner purchased the property with plans to renovate the building and operate it as a hotel with residences, a rooftop bar and a ground-floor restaurant.

Find out more about Price Tower ›

The Kennedy Center, Washington, DC, by Edward Durell Stone

The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC is the subject of ongoing controversy after Donald Trump ousted its leadership in February 2025 and proposed an overhaul of the exterior. Trump also affixed his own name to the building, which was later removed.

There is an ongoing back and forth about the president's legal right to reshape the building, and groups such as the AIA have joined a lawsuit against the government in hopes of preserving the original design.

Find out more about The Kennedy Center ›

Victor Lundy House, Texas, by Victor Lundy 

A group of preservationists including the Texas Historical Foundation, Houston Mod, Docomomo US and Preservation Houston won a hard-fought battle to save American architect Victor Lundy's personal residence in Houston, Texas late last year.

With the support of the group, buyers Dan and Carol Price purchased the house, saving it from demolition. Preservation Houston says the plan is to "restore the property and explore possibilities for its continued use and preservation".

Find out more about Victor Lundy House ›

Elgin Mental Health Center Medical and Surgical building, Illinois, by Bertrand Goldberg

The circular Elgin Mental Health Center Medical and Surgical Building outside of Chicago was being eyed for demolition early last year after decades of disuse.

As of now, there is no widely reported timeline for the demolition, but the building is "worth preserving" according to Geoffrey Goldberg, son of building architect Bertrand Goldberg.

Find out more about the Elgin Mental Health Center Medical and Surgical Building ›

Malibu house, California, by Tadao Ando

A Malibu beach house by Japanese architect Tadao Ando was stripped down to its concrete structure by musician Ye and wife Bianca Censori in 2024.

Ye sold the structure after failing to convert it into a "bunker" as intended, and the current owner is struggling to sell the building before it forecloses, according to Architectural Digest.

Find out more about the Tadao Ando Malibu house ›

item.content:encoded:
International architecture studio SOM has released designs of the 20-storey 934 Central Street data centre in Kansas City, USA, with a facade configured to "feel at home within its downtown context".

The 20-storey skyscraper will be built in the heart of Kansas City on a 0.23-acre site that is currently occupied by the Western Newspaper Union Building.

Developed by Miami-based Revitalization Unlimited, the structure will incorporate floors for data systems, cooling systems, and power generation, all arrayed vertically, a marked departure from the massive horizontal structures that have dominated the news cycle in the wake of the AI boom.

"A vertical closed loop"

"Unlike conventional data centers, which typically occupy large, horizontal footprints, 934 Central Street envisions a vertical data center for a dense downtown setting, closer to where people live and work," said a spokesperson for SOM.

"The proposal stacks data floors, power infrastructure, cooling systems, and public amenities within a 20-story tower on a compact 0.23-acre site, creating a vertical closed loop of power, water, and cooling."

The structure will feature an earth-coloured masonry facade with large panes of glass, even on floors dedicated to the data modules. It will have an external core allowing for more room in the interior of the skyscraper.

On ground level, SOM has planned for 4,700 square feet (436 square metres) of shops.

The commercial element was designed with the relatively standard cladding system to make the skyscraper align with the urban context, according to SOM.

"Designed to feel at home within its downtown context, the building draws from the vertical proportions, repetitive bays, and masonry character of surrounding commercial buildings," said SOM.

Increasing data centre reliance

Likely in response to recent uproar about water and energy usage in data centers, the studio has included plans for on-site power generation, reportedly from natural gas cells. A diagram of the skyscraper supplied by SOM states that the power system is "100 per cent independent from the grid".

It also states that the water will be internally cycled through equipment on the upper floors, with evaporative cooling elements shown as a feature at the bulkhead.

SOM claimed that the proximity to the urban systems that will likely utilise the data centre's output is a reason for its location.

"As cities around the world become increasingly reliant on data centers, locating this infrastructure within urban areas offers both efficient proximity to the industries and networks it serves and an opportunity for these buildings to contribute positively to surrounding communities," said the studio.

The structure also answers a question raised by many of the massive data centres going up across the country – what will happen to these structures if the demand for computation decreases?

"The tower is also configured to adapt over time, with a side core, regular structural grid, and generous floor-to-floor heights that support future conversion to residential, office, or mixed-use space as technological needs evolve," said SOM.

However, there has been community pushback, with local outlets reporting locals pushing back on grounds of the "speculative" nature of the project and the potential for urban heat island effects, which are reportedly exacerbated by data centres.

Read:

Plant-covered Rio AI City set to be Latin America's largest data centre

Locals also expressed concern over the demolition of the Western Newspaper Union Building, with the City Planning Commission scheduled to review the project today, 5 August 2026.

Recently, Gensler designed a massive hyperscale data centre in Utah and a data centre was approved as part of the Truman Brewery development in east London.

item.content:encoded:
A vast grid of red scaffolding surrounds The Reclaimed Pavilion, a temporary events space in India designed by local studio Kanan Modi Associates using materials that were salvaged from local construction sites.

Commissioned by real estate firm Jayabheri Group for a rapidly developing neighbourhood in Hyderabad, the 1,500-square-metre pavilion contains work and events spaces alongside a show home for a nearby apartment block, The Pinnacle.

Given its temporary nature, Kanan Modi Associates looked to use salvaged and repurposed materials wherever possible. This included gabion walls made from construction debris, bricks made from excavated earth and reclaimed corrugated metal sheets, all assembled to be easily dismantled.

Surrounding the entire site is a gridded framework made from repurposed scaffolding, which has been painted a deep shade of red and used to support a series of zigzagging jute fabric canopies that shade its external areas.

"Rather than asking what new materials could be introduced, every design decision began with the question: what already exists that can be given a second life?" Kanan Modi Associates founder Kana Modi told Dezeen.

"Equally important was planning for the pavilion's eventual dismantling. The scaffolding system will return to construction use, corrugated metal sheets will be reused, and the excavated earth blocks can return to the ground as fill."

Entering into a pale brick-paved reception area with a sunken pit at its centre, The Reclaimed Pavilion is organised as a row of flexible gathering and events spaces, lined by more compartmentalised, privates spaces for work and meetings.

Dividing the pavilion's three main spaces are large gabion walls made from construction debris, which extend beyond the pavilion's edges to help shade and separate its external areas.

Read:

Dum-Dum Lab constructs lakeside pavilion as environmental classroom

"A series of open gathering areas, shaded seating zones and flexible event spaces flow around a central water body, encouraging movement and informal interaction," Modi told Dezeen.

"The flexible layout allows the pavilion to seamlessly accommodate art exhibitions, talks, performances, community events and informal gatherings, adapting to a diverse range of public programmes."

The central spaces are flanked by a stepped steel deck and shallow L-shaped pool that wraps the pavilion's southwestern edge, and a more enclosed external plaza to the north, which is shaded by the scaffolding canopy and overlooks another pool of water.

Atop these pools of water, the scaffolding grid is echoed by a grid of pale concrete stepping stones, which were cast in-situ in an irregular checkerboard layout.

At its western end, the show flat sits separated from the main space of the pavilion, occupying a contrasting white volume that is also encased within the pavilion's scaffolding.

Other projects in India that have given a new life to salvaged construction waste include the Belgaluru studio of design practice Multitude of Sins, which made use of scrap metal and acrylic sheets, chains and even door knobs.

The photography is by Fernando Guerra.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio MAD has unveiled Shenzhen Bay Culture Square in China, a design museum formed of stone-like volumes perched atop an undulating green roof.

Situated in Houhai in Shenzhen's Nanshan District, MAD designed the museum to be a hub for design and culture as well as a coastal public space for city residents to enjoy.

"Much of my work is guided by the same question: can public space be more open and equal?" said MAD founder Ma Yansong.

"Shenzhen is a young, efficient city, and this site was entirely reclaimed from the sea," he continued. "How can our design turn ancient nature into people's imagination of the future, and make a large cultural building feel intimate, in service of human experience?"

Flanked by a cluster of skyscrapers on one side and Talent Park on the other side, the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square contains exhibition galleries, education spaces, a design library and a multifunctional theatre.

An undulating green roof spans over the site, concealing much of the museum space below ground and providing winding routes between the city and coastline.

Atop the green roof are boulder-like volumes clad in polished granite, which decrease in height from a 28-metre-tall gallery at the city end of the site, to a long, low-slung domed gallery positioned towards the adjacent park.

The building was designed to lie low in the landscape to stay out of the flight path of migratory birds travelling the East Asian-Australasian Flyway.

Read:

MAD clads bulbous science museum with silver-toned polymer panels in China

"By placing the building volumes beneath the landscape, the project leaves the ground to nature, creating an open waterfront park where people can freely walk, explore, and linger," said MAD.

"Visitors enter from every direction, climb the gentle slopes, follow the winding roof paths, and reach lookouts over the bay."

In the subterranean galleries, the concrete structure was left exposed, with lights and services tucked into the ceiling.

A ring-shaped atrium encircles one of the stone-like volumes, connecting the underground galleries and drawing daylight in.

A shallow pool sits at the centre of the site, and an outdoor plaza was designed to host outdoor performances, art markets and festivals.

Native species of planting populate the roof, and the landscaping abutting the wetland area of the adjacent park gradually steps down towards the shore, designed to blend into it rather than forming a hard border.

Other projects recently completed by MAD in China include a bulbous science museum in Haikou and a curving headquarters building in Shenzhen.

The photography is courtesy of MAD.

item.content:encoded:
Asca Studio and Relief Gallery joined forces to create the interiors of the Ómós guesthouse outside Abbeyleix, Ireland, which was converted from a ruin into a welcoming space filled with tactile materials.

The 16-room guesthouse is located in a formerly dilapidated Victorian house that was renovated by local studio Ryan W Kennihan Architects.

It also has a dedicated restaurant, set in a new building that was designed by the same studio and informed by Irish farmsteads.

Interior architects Asca Studio and Relief Gallery were challenged to create an interior that would make the separate spaces feel like two halves of a whole.

"Although both the guesthouse and restaurant carry the same spirit of hospitality central to how clients and staff move throughout the space, the two concepts naturally differ," Asca Studio co-founder Cassandra Bradfield told Dezeen.

"However, material palettes as well as small systems like integrated symbols within the hardware, furniture pieces, and woodwork create a sense of internal symbology and consistency throughout."

The two studios used tactile materials throughout Ómós' interior, contrasting local stone with plaster and wood.

"The foundational materials are Kilkenny limestone, ash, and lime plaster: the limestone adds weight and longevity, the ash character and warmth, and the lime plaster reflects light and absorbs sound because it is so textural," Relief Gallery founder Rebecca Norberg told Dezeen.

"The limestone was used on surfaces exposed heavily to the elements and wear, for example outdoors, on public entrance floors, vanity basins and shower trays, whilst we used wood to contrast this on more protected floors, joinery, furniture, doors and accessories."

As the guesthouse part of Ómós was "essentially a ruin", according to Norberg, the designers worked to preserve and reinstate typical period details from the Victorian house.

These included fireplaces as well as skirtings and mouldings, with the layout of the three front rooms also recreated.

The overall concept behind the guesthouse was to both celebrate its surroundings outside Abbeyleix, Ireland's oldest estate town, and make it stand out.

"Ómós is an Irish word meaning homage, duty and respect – the brief was to celebrate people, place and produce, and make the guesthouse and restaurant a destination," Norberg said.

"We wanted it to feel like nothing else in Ireland and, at the same time, deeply familiar to anyone who grew up there."

Read:

Reds shingles create "sense of personality and wonder" at Cucu cabin by Studio Bucky

Asca and Relief Gallery also added new details that fit the historic feel of the building, including a stone basin in an entryway.

"The stone basin was a new addition to the space, which functions as a 'boot wash' and filling station for both guests and staff to use," Bradfield explained.

Ómós has a warm, muted colour palette, with soft beige and green hues taking centre stage. This was inspired by the surrounding nature of County Laois in central Ireland.

"The colour palette is a mixture of tones directly taken from the site, inspired to reflect or enhance the natural light coming in, and lean into the energy of each specific space," Bradfield said.

"For instance, one suite and ensuite located in close proximity to the main garden features about 10 shades of green and blue taken directly from the vignette you see outside, and then there's a sunny yellow suite located at the front of the property that mirrors the light streaming in."

For the furniture, Bradfield and Norberg sourced vernacular vintage pieces, which were combined with custom designs by their studios and work by Irish craftsmen, as well as Scandinavian furniture.

"Standouts include the hedge chairs in the restaurant lounge, the dining chairs by Michael Murphy and De La Espada's Arts and Crafts Sideboard in Suite 01," she said.

Overall, the designers believe the final design fulfilled the vision that they set out to create.

"Irish visitors tell us they have never experienced anything like it here, and that, at the same time, the breakfast room reminds them of their grandmother's cottage kitchen, and that's how we know the design works," Norberg concluded.

Other recent Irish projects featured on Dezeen include an elevated extension in Dublin and an off-grid cabin clad in red shingles.

The photography is by Irina Boersma César Machado.

item.content:encoded:
Researchers in China have created a textile from living mycelium that is self-cleaning, near self-repairing and can be coloured or made UV protective through "plug-and-play" add-ons of different fungi or yeast.

The breakthrough from the researchers at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology is a type of engineered living material (ELM) – a material built off living organisms that stay active even after they're fabricated into their final form.

This distinguishes it from most contemporary uses of mycelium, which involve drying and effectively killing the fungus to produce a stable, non-growing material that has become a popular emerging alternative to plastic packaging and vinyl.

By working with living but dormant cordyceps militaris fungus instead, the researchers have been able to take advantage of its biological functions. The result is a material that is self-renewing and responsive to its environment, in ways that could one day transform architecture and clothing – as seen in a prototype dress created together with material innovation company Peelshere.

It can also be adapted by mixing in other fungi or yeast, lead researcher Ke Li and her team detail in a paper in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances.

In it, they describe a "programmable fungal platform" where mycelium is treated like a modular system, with the sheet material forming a base structure and extra biological abilities, such as colour and UV resistance, becoming "plug-and-play" add-ons via other organisms.

This gets their textile closer to the self-repair, environmental responsiveness and controllable functionality that is the promise of engineered living materials, they argue.

"While synthetic biology has greatly expanded the functional capabilities of ELMs, a persistent challenge lies in integrating autonomous structural assembly with sustained biological activity at macroscopic scales," the scientists write.

"Achieving such integration is essential for practical applications, from adaptive textiles to architectural biomaterials, where mechanical robustness, spatial uniformity and scalable fabrication must converge with engineered biological function."

Read:

Algae "biocells" powered by photosynthesis could replace disposable batteries

The ELM's self-renewing and semi-repairing functionality comes from the mycelium base structure. Following drying at 45 degrees, the material is not quite living and not quite dead, but instead in a "low-metabolic, dormant-like state", Li told Dezeen, meaning it is not actively growing.

However, new growth can be triggered by applying a nutrient solution of potato water, leading the dormant mycelium to germinate, send out new fungal filaments and renew the material's surface.

When this nutrient solution is applied over a hole, along with a small patch of fresh fungus, it triggers the living cells to grow across the gap, seamlessly repairing the surface without any adhesives or stitching. The material is also naturally self-cleaning, as it is hydrophobic.

The blue colour and UV resistance, meanwhile, come from brewer's yeast – also known as saccharomyces cerevisiae – and aspergillus niger fungus, respectively. These are mixed in with the cordyceps militaris at the beginning and simply co-cultured, avoiding the need for genetic engineering.

A prototype dress has been made out of the scientists' material by Berlin-based Peelshere, whose founder YouYang Song is a friend of Li's. Song developed the conceptual and aesthetic design of the dress, while her China-based colleague Ruochen Wang took care of the cutting and construction.

The dress features several versions of the material, including some co-cultured with brewer's yeast for the consistently self-pigmented blue shade in the body of the garment.

Li told Dezeen that the material is suitable for applications such as conceptual fashion, accessories, decorative textile surfaces, exhibition pieces and biodegradable packaging.

"Its distinctive surface texture, biological colouring, controlled repair and biodegradability may be particularly useful in applications where visual expression and a defined product lifetime are important," she said.

"Further improvements in durability, moisture resistance, safety and manufacturing consistency would be needed before it could be considered for routine clothing or permanent architectural use."

Peelsphere's main product is a plant-based and waterproof leather alternative made of fruit peels and algae.

Photography by Ke Li.

item.content:encoded:
Local studio River Architects has designed a wood-clad structure to Passive House standards, orienting gabled volumes around a pond in New York's Hudson Valley.

Known as the China Pond Passive House, the 4,318-square-foot (400-square-metre) home sits on a wooded 2.2-acre property in Carmel, New York.

River Architects, which is based in nearby Cold Spring, completed the house in November 2025, replacing an earlier residence with a similar footprint.

The studio built the new home from the ground up but didn't approach the site as a blank slate.

"We wanted to maintain that sense of evolution in the new house, a decision which also helps break up the overall form so it doesn't seem overwhelming," James Hartford, principal and partner of River Architects, told Dezeen.

"The result is a playful push and pull in massing, resulting in unusual in-between places and quirky angles."

Connecting with the site's existing infrastructure and stonework, the house works in dialogue with its surrounding trees and views of the water, capturing the spirit of the original house – a collection of spaces that balance a sense of retreat with the encouragement to gather.

In order to echo the additive nature of camp buildings and reduce the scale of the house, the massing is broken into a series of smaller volumes.

Two gabled forms – a two-level bar that faces east and west and a three-level bar that is rotated slightly – are joined by a flat-roofed wedge.

The forms are wrapped in reclaimed cypress and Douglas fir above the native stone foundation that is partially embedded in the sloped site.

Inside, the team worked to recreate the feeling of the original library in the great room to be both intimate and expansive for entertaining, with views and daylight. Private sleeping spaces are ganged to the southern side of the house, while the communal areas blend between the central and northern portions.

The lower level is more informal with recreation space, a sauna and access to a large deck that mimics the terrace on the main level.

"A central stone chimney serves as the physical and social heart of the home, organizing the primary living and outdoor spaces while anchoring views and activity around it," Hartford said.

"The house opens to the landscape, balancing expansive lake views with moments of privacy and shelter."

 

In order to achieve Passive House certification, sustainable elements were embedded in the project from the outset.

The house features a highly insulated and airtight building envelope, triple-pane glazing, careful solar orientation and shading strategies that reduce energy demand while improving comfort.

The locally sourced wood reduced carbon impact and maintenance, while active systems – all-electric heat pumps, energy recovery ventilation and infrastructure for renewable energy generation – contribute to the performance.

"Together, these measures enabled the project to achieve Phius certification and provide exceptional indoor comfort with significantly reduced operational energy use and no fossil fuel use," the studio said.

Other recently built single-family Passive Houses include a retrofitted terrace house in Queens by CO Adaptive, a courtyard home in Chile by Paralelo Transversal and a retrofitted Victorian home with a "fabric first" approach in London by GS Architecture.

The photography is by Pamela Cook.

New York studios Schlaich Bergermann Partner and Snøhetta have replaced an ageing bridge in Upstate New York with a steel half-arch span that is mounted on one side of a gorge and cantilevers across to the other side.

The Sentry Bridge replaces a decaying structure of the same name located in Watkins Glen State Park in the Finger Lakes region of New York.

The bridge is wedged between two cavernous rock walls among the park's twisting, mossy trails that navigate along Watkins Glen gorge, and overlooks a low riverbed at the base of a waterfall.

It marks the beginning of the gorge path, and, according to the team, "sets a tone for adventure".

"The bridge and pathways honour the histories and craft traditions of the gorge, protect unique cliff and creek ecosystems. and heighten the experience of stone and water," said Snøhetta project director Matt McMahon.

The bridge was fabricated locally and is made of a stainless steel structure. It is primarily affixed to the north side of the gorge, where the bedrock is stronger, and cantilevers 46 feet (14 metres) to the other side.

The main structure was pre-fabricated and slotted into the slim site via crane.

The team then finished the bridge with black locust wood rails, concrete formed of rough-sawn hemlock, and a bluestone landing.

Read:

Moxon Architects adds "functional and graceful" bridge to Scottish highlands

Custom bronze castings of local flora and fauna such as an endangered dragonfly, a rare plant, and a model of the historic arch bridge were also distributed throughout the site for visitors to "pause and examine" the regional heritage of the area.

According to the team, the bridge frames views of the surrounding waterfalls and "heightens awareness of the mist and shifting light".

"The bridge demonstrates how thoughtful engineering can support both performance and experience," said Schlaich Bergermann Partner managing director Michael Stein.

"By developing a lightweight, cantilevered structure that could be prefabricated and installed with minimal impact on the gorge, we were able to create a resilient crossing that responds to the site's environmental sensitivities while enhancing the journey through one of New York’s most remarkable landscapes."

Other recently completed pedestrian bridges include a footbridge in France that spans over a 19th-century viaduct over the River Tarn and a low-lying bridge over a Belgian river.

item.content:encoded:
Agricultural barns and sheds informed the corrugated metal-clad volumes of House in a Clearing, a house in East Sussex completed by UK studio TaylorHare Architects.

When the clients purchased the site nestled in a woodland clearing near Uckfield, it was occupied by a small structure but already had planning permission for a much larger, two-storey dwelling.

The new owners, however, sought a quieter design that would feel more connected to the landscape, leading to TaylorHare Architects creating a cluster of three single-storey barns organised around a central courtyard informed by traditional farmsteads.

"Every design decision was measured against a simple question: did it strengthen the relationship between house and landscape?" director and project principal Christopher Taylor told Dezeen.

"Drawing on the character of rural agricultural steadings, the composition creates a home that feels both grounded and quietly expressive," he continued.

At the centre of House in a Clearing, a slightly larger building clad in black metal contains the main social spaces, which overlook both the paved courtyard and surrounding landscape through large windows.

A snug leads through into the bedroom wing, where a row of more intimate spaces sit off a long corridor and have also been given minimal, white finishes to emphasise external views through large openings framed in black metal.

To the south, a glazed link connects the living areas to an ancillary building, which contains a garage, home gym and guest room and is finished with a gable end of brickwork that the studio said "anchors the building in the landscape".

Read:

Charles Gillespie Architecture completes Somerset house with wildlife-friendly colonnade

All of the volumes are united by their finish of corrugated metal, which covers both their walls and roofs. According to the studio, this was chosen for its ability to make the home feel "both contemporary and deeply rooted in its setting".

The internal finishes of the home were kept purposefully minimal, with white walls and high gable ceilings complemented by pale oak timber in the bedrooms and stone paving in the kitchen and bathroom.

"White-rendered walls and natural timber create calm, light-filled spaces where the changing landscape, rather than the architecture itself, becomes the primary focus," Taylor told Dezeen.

"Ultimately, the materials were never intended to make a statement in their own right. Instead, they work together to create a building that feels enduring, familiar and quietly connected to its place."

Other recent homes in the UK that have taken cues from agricultural buildings include the transformation of a former tractor shed in Dorset into a low-carbon home by architecture practice Bindloss Dawes.

The photography is by Nick Dearden.

Located on Queen's Road in Hong Kong's Central district, the hotel was first established a decade ago. It recently reopened after the completion of interior renovation

item.content:encoded:
Designer Joyce Wang has completed an interior renovation at the Mandarin Oriental The Landmark hotel in Hong Kong, designed to evoke the feel of living in a colonial mansion.

Located on Queen's Road in Hong Kong's Central district, the hotel was first established a decade ago. It recently reopened after the completion of interior renovation by Joyce Wang Studio and a new facade design by Neri&Hu.

Joyce Wang Studio referenced Hong Kong’s historic architecture and skyline when designing the hotel, whose interior was informed by the city's colonial country manors.

"We took inspiration from the colonial country manors frequented by the Tai Kwuns of a bygone era to celebrate the beauty of these historic homes that still fascinate today," Wang, principal of her eponymous studio, told Dezeen. "Our vision this time has a greater focus on local relevance and the heritage of the building."

The studio also aimed to fuse art into the hotel.

"We also used art as an integral part of our philosophy for the space, with a commitment to adding local flavour. The artwork program is rigorous in that there is a story behind each piece," Wang added.

The hotel lobby features a mix of materials including stone, timber and textured wallcoverings. Custom eglomisé glass was added as detailing to create a contemporary atmosphere.

Terracotta tones within the space nod to Hong Kong's colonial architecture and were combined with a touch of green and orange in response to the city's lush green parks.

Throughout the hotel, a collection of artworks was carefully curated to create an authentic lived-in residence.

Artwork, objects and accessories scattered around an undulating staircase, artwork bays and sculptural plinths invite guests to pause and interact with them while venturing into the space.

Custom artworks capturing Hong Kong's signature skyline were created by the studio and integrated into carpet designs, tapestries and the églomise glass located at the lobby, as well as lifts and guestroom corridors.

According to the Hong Kong-based studio, the artistic intervention aims to celebrate the hotel's prominent location in the city, while presenting a series of treasured objects as if collected over time for one's own home.

Joyce Wang Studio aimed to create an intimate and residential feel in Mandarin Oriental The Landmark's 109 rooms and suites.

Details include bespoke wallcoverings by wallpaper brand Fromental, featuring hand-painted and silk elements, and cracked gesso wall finishes. Custom rugs on top of timber floors reference Hong Kong's historic brickwork.

A new communal bar was reimagined as a contemporary family gathering space. Here, the design is defined by a backdrop featuring patinated brass, verdigris, and bronze panels, allowing the space to adapt seamlessly between day and night service.

Ceiling lamps in matching patinated finishes pay homage to the domestic lighting found in the historic mansions of Yuen Long, a town in the western north of Hong Kong's New Territories, where several notable historic mansions and grand residences are located.

Fluted jade-toned tiles wrap the bar front, recreating the roofline silhouettes of traditional housing.

Tangerine and cherry-toned bar chairs contrast with the bar table. Their backs are adorned with a crest-like motif that symbolises a contemporary family emblem inherited through generations.

"For this latest renovation, we were inspired by the identity of our hotel as a pied-à-terre for our guests to feel the pulse of Hong Kong, intimately. The curation of pieces are windows into expressions of our city through lenses of both local and international, emerging and established artists," said Wang.

"As you journey through the hotel, we hope these storied perspectives fill you with curiosity and contemplation, at the ready to strike up conversations," she continued.

Read:

Neri&Hu wraps Hong Kong hotel in "urban tapestry" facade

For the hotel spa, Joyce Wang Studio added design details informed by breathwork and calligraphy to create a sense of calm.

Custom flooring patterns were designed to mimic the natural rhythm of inhalation and exhalation, allowing guests to connect with the space as if it is breathing with them.

Two distinct wood veneers were paired together within the gym, yoga, and pilates studios, creating a balanced, organic environment that encourages a sense of focused calm.

The sinuous and fluid lines on the ceiling and decorative screens aim to recreate the brush strokes of Chinese calligraphy.

The hotel has officially reopened since June, while the spa will fully reopen later this year.

Established in 2011, Joyce Wang Studio is known for luxury hospitality and residential design, with offices in London and Hong Kong.

Elsewhere in Hong Kong, Studio Paolo Ferrari designed a "timeless futurism" cocktail bar, while the Dragon-i nightclub renovated by local interior designer Pirajean Lees captured the romantic atmosphere of director Wong Kar Wai's films.

The photography is by Common Studio.

item.content:encoded:
Wood, aluminium and artworks made from reused textiles were used to create speaker brand Dynaudio's new showroom in Copenhagen, which local studio Norm Architects has filled with wooden furniture by Japanese manufacturer Karimoku.

The showroom is located in Copenhagen's picturesque, central Indre By neighbourhood, in a former flagship store for Danish shoe brand Notabene that was also designed by Norm Architects.

For  Dynaudio, however, the studio wanted to create an interior that would reference the brand's products.

"We looked to create an environment where both the material and colour palette of the space is experienced as if you imagined the speaker components unfolded and fitted into the space itself," Norm Architects partner Frederik Werner told Dezeen.

"Elements of wood, aluminium and textile act as counterparts to the concrete surfaces of the building and create an environment that is both raw and soft."

The 250-square-metre showroom was designed in collaboration with Dynaudio and branding agency Kontrapunkt.

It is spread over three floors, including a wooden mezzanine floor that holds a large table and chairs for meetings, all connected by a sculptural, zigzagging wooden staircase.

Since the space was designed for a speaker company, Norm Architects also aimed to include materials with acoustic properties.

The most notable are perhaps the large, striking black-and-white artworks that decorate the walls, which were made by Amsterdam studio Buro Belén using recycled fabrics from textile brand Kvadrat.

"Besides the textile murals, we added elements of eelgrass panels from Danish manufacturer Søuld in the ceiling as they benefit both the acoustic experience and create an overall healthier environment, by for instance stabilising the humidity of the space," Werner said.

As well as the eelgrass panels and recycled-textile artworks, Norm Architects also collaborated with Corkinho, a Portuguese brand that makes furniture and other elements in cork, which were added to the interior to also help with the acoustics.

"We used cork volumes as 'vibration buffers' between the speakers and aluminium plinths," Werner explained.

The furniture in the showroom was supplied by Karimoku since the Japanese manufacturer already had a strong working relationship with Dynaudio, having produced all the wooden elements for Keiji Ashizawa's Book Shelf speaker and the louvres for the Opus One soundbar.

Read:

Norm Architecture draws on "Scandinavian simplicity" for Danish gallery interior

Among the Karimoku pieces on display are dark-wood tables and chairs, as well as comfy sofas and custom-made acoustic designs.

"We found it natural to invite them into this case and to design a collection of furniture that fulfilled and heightened the listening experience and curated service concept in general," Werner said.

The studio also designed a specific listening area in the basement for visitors to get the full audio experience.

"In the basement, guests will be able to experience the full capabilities of Dynaudio, in a small acoustically optimised cinema-like listening room – which I can highly recommend," Werner concluded.

Other recent projects by Norm Architects include the first Audo House in New York and a gallery space on the Danish island of Bornholm.

The photography is by Karl Tranberg Knudsen.

item.content:encoded:
A stripped-back interior of concrete surfaces and timber joinery lets sustainable production practices take centre stage at Melbourne's Contraband Coffee cafe and roastery, designed by architecture studio Taylor Knights.

The cafe is located in Melbourne's buzzy Brunswick East neighbourhood and is the second Contraband Coffee branch to be designed by Taylor Knights, which also devised the interiors of the company's inaugural site in nearby Preston.

As part of a move to eradicate fossil fuels from its roasting and distribution process, Contraband Coffee has set up this location to be entirely solar powered.

Inside there's an all-electric coffee bean roaster, and deliveries will be made with electric vans. The company also partners with local business Reground to recycle its used soft plastic packaging, coffee grounds and chaff – the dried skin surrounding coffee beans that falls off during the roasting process.

Taylor Knights was asked to reflect this sustainability-focused ethos in the cafe's design.

"For us, the project demonstrates that environmental responsibility doesn't need to be expressed through technology alone; it can also be found in the careful reuse of buildings, materials and places that already exist," Taylor Knights' director Peter Knights told Dezeen.

The cafe occupies a former industrial warehouse, and although the double-storey brick building was structurally sound, Taylor Knights said it felt "dark, inward-looking and largely isolated from its surroundings".

The studio decided to puncture a sequence of glazed openings along the northern facade to allow more natural light into the plan and create a better visual connection to the newly established courtyard at the side of the building.

The rest of the interior was retained, with the existing concrete ceiling beams and slab flooring cleaned where necessary.

"The material palette was guided by a desire to reveal rather than replace," explained Knights. "The restrained palette allows texture and material honesty to take precedence, with planting and subtle green accents softening the industrial character and strengthening the connection to the landscape beyond."

Read:

Taylor Knights opens up garden views at Melbourne home with glass-fronted extension

Customers make their orders at a chunky service counter crafted from locally sourced timber. Coffee machines stand at one end, while the other houses a built-in glass case for baked goods.

Next to the counter are a few tables accompanied by sage green chairs; directly behind stands a curtain wall, also constructed from local timber.

Half of it is inlaid with glass so that customers can see through to the room where the electric roaster is and watch staff process the coffee beans.

Double doors lead out to the courtyard, conceived by Taylor Knights with the help of landscape architects TCL.

At its centre is a communal high table and stools, but customers can also perch on one of the benches or circular seating platforms. Cylindrical concrete planters stand dotted throughout.

Additional seating is offered at the front of the cafe, where the building's old car parking area was populated with more benches, supported by aluminium frames repurposed by Taylor Knights from its 2021 installation Pond[er] at the National Gallery of Victoria.

The wall beside the entrance doors has also been decorated with a cartoonish mural by artist Chris Costa.

Beyond cafes, Taylor Knights has completed several residential projects in and around Melbourne. Examples include a bungalow in Brunswick West, which features a glass-fronted extension quietly inspired by a Wassily Kandinsky painting.

item.content:encoded:
A glass-walled pavilion sandwiched between historic buildings is the leading feature of an Oregon art museum revamp, which was designed by US studios Hennebery Eddy Architects and Vinci Hamp Architects to improve the visitor experience.

Spanning two urban blocks, the Portland Art Museum is located in the city's downtown district.

It primarily consists of two historic buildings: the Belluschi Building, designed by architect Pietro Belluschi and completed in 1932, and the Mark Building, designed by Frederick Fritsch and dating to 1926. The latter originally served as a masonic temple and was acquired by the museum in the 1990s.

Local studio Hennebery Eddy Architects and Chicago-based Vinci Hamp Architects were tasked with updating the museum's existing buildings and adding a connector building – with the overall goal to provide a "more streamlined and holistic visitor experience".

For the connector building, the team conceived the Mark Rothko Pavilion, named after the abstract expressionist artist who grew up in Portland.

The multi-storey, 24,000-square-foot (223-square-metre) structure sits between the two historic buildings.

"The pavilion establishes a new main entry and links previously discontinuous circulation and disparate floor elevations, creating an intuitive and cohesive venue for art," the team said.

Rather than a simple box, the pavilion has setbacks that give it a more dynamic look. Along one side, the team cut away a portion of the ground level to form a breezeway for pedestrians and cyclists.

"The passageway connects the east and west entry plazas, where key pieces from the museum's sculpture collection are accessible to the public, establishing a uniquely Portland feature that offers passersby sheltered views into galleries and extends the museum experience into the public realm," the team said.

Designed to respect the context, the pavilion has glazed walls lined with long, metal mullions and white-ceramic frit.

These elements are a nod to the historic neighbours – specifically the travertine trim found on the Belluschi Building and the vertical elements that characterise the Mark Building.

"The crystalline, contemporary form of the Rothko Pavilion projects a distinctly modernist character but respects its historic partners," the team said.

Within the pavilion, extensive glazing provides a connection to the surrounding neighbourhood. A restrained material palette includes white oak flooring in galleries and granite pavers in other areas.

The pavilion's ground level contains the museum's Community Commons, which is free to enter and was conceived "as a gathering space for all".

Upper-level terraces offer visitors the chance "to step outside and take in Portland's skyline and iconic South Park Blocks", the latter a reference to a 12-block stretch of green space.

In addition to the new Rothko Pavilion, the museum project also included renovations to the existing structures, with a focus on improving the galleries in a way that "puts art first".

In the Belluschi Building, traditional-style galleries have been refreshed. The team also added a volume that holds an upper-floor gallery and a receiving dock on the lower level.

Within the Mark Building, the team "simplified" the galleries and updated an auditorium.

Read:

Vacant supermarket in Portland converted into library facility by Hennebery Eddy

It also converted a library into a 2,700-square-foot (251-square-metre) gallery dedicated to contemporary work by emerging artists. The library was moved to another part of the building.

The project also entailed a revamp of the museum's cafe, store, and spaces for the conservation and education departments.

Overall, the renovation and expansion have greatly improved the visitor experience and solved challenges that have plagued the museum for decades, according to the team.

"The $111 million expansion is one of the most significant capital investments in the arts in the history of Oregon," the team said.

"The updated campus balances the needs of its urban neighbourhood and the city and reinforces the museum's role as a cultural beacon of downtown Portland."

Other recent projects in Portland include the conversion of a vacant supermarket into a library facility by Hennebery Eddy and a ZGF-designed expansion of the main terminal at Portland International Airport, which features a giant mass-timber roof.

item.content:encoded:
Plans unveiled by architecture studio Buckley Gray Yeoman for offices, homes and a data centre near Brick Lane in London have been approved.

Planned for three sites in the east London neighbourhood, the Truman Brewery masterplan will comprise eight buildings designed by Buckley Gray Yeoman (BGY), alongside London-based studios Carmody Groarke, Morris+Company and Henley Halebrown.

Approved last week by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, the contentious proposal will include a 5,200-square-metre data centre designed by Morris+Company.

Additionally, plans for 35,000-square-metres of office, retail and community space will include the redevelopment of the existing Truman Brewery. This will see a two-story extension and public space added to the building's grade II-listed Boiler House.

Forty four homes will also be built as part of the development, six of which will be social housing specifically designed to accommodate larger Bangladeshi-heritage families.

Renders of the proposal reveal a series of multi-storey buildings flanked by courtyards and signposted by the Truman Brewery chimney.

Plans originally submitted by BGY in 2024 were strongly opposed by the Tower Hamlets Council and local campaign group Save Brick Lane, which argued the development could displace local residents and businesses.

Despite controversy over the plans, the UK Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested that the Truman Brewery proposal will bring "increased footfall" to local businesses and generate employment.

Rayner and Labour minister Matthew Pennycook also praised the data centre for its "very significant" public benefits and "associated economic benefits".

Read:

Images of relocated London Museum by Stanton Williams and Asif Khan revealed

In response to the approved plans, Save Brick Lane expressed that it was "deeply disappointed".

Tower Hamlets mayor Lutfur Rahman also criticised the lack of social housing, noting a "missed opportunity" to address the borough's "acute housing crisis", according to the BBC.

"Against that backdrop, development of this scale delivering only six homes for social rent falls significantly short of addressing local need," Rahman said.

In other architecture news, plug-in solar panels, which can be fitted onto balconies, are set to become available in the UK and the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard has been launched by certification company Bureau Veritas in a bid to minimise greenwashing.

item.content:encoded:
Irregularly placed and mismatched openings puncture the terracotta-toned, double-layered exterior of 100 Windows, a multigenerational home in Vietnam designed by local architecture practice Inrestudio.

Designed for two generations and three households – a couple, their two sons and the sons' families – the 639-square-metre home is located close to the Red River in the suburbs of Hanoi.

Responding to both the region's tropical climate and the likelihood of extensive development in the future, Inrestudio wrapped the home with a double-layered exterior to create pockets of private outdoor space and help filter air through its interiors.

"The project is shaped around ambiguity," studio founder Niko told Dezeen. "The suburb itself is ambiguous, neither city nor countryside, and so is its future; even 'family' is an ambiguous unit here, three households whose composition will keep changing,"

"As a vessel for this indeterminate program, an abstract house form retains a minimal symbol of 'house', while the many openings set the building apart from its neighbours," he added.

While the home features multiple windows, its name 100 Windows was intended "as a symbolic expression of abundance, rather than a literal count of one hundred windows," Niko said.

The home is elevated atop a slightly setback base of dark, textured concrete. A floor paved in basalt unites an external patio with a swimming pool and the ground floor living, dining and kitchen areas.

Above, two storeys of bedrooms and a top floor with a second living, dining and kitchen area have been designed to adapt to a variety of family arrangements, with the whole being encased within the home's distinctive double-skin facade.

Read:

Perforated brick wall fronts breezy home in Vietnam by Live Out Studio

Numerous openings puncture both layers of this facade. Many of these openings align to give the home's windows unobstructed views, while some have been offset to provide shade and privacy to recessed balconies and thin terraces.

Inrestudio also used the additional thickness of this double-layered exterior to create shelving, desks, storage and ventilation channels that help to cool the interiors, which have been finished with dark timber floors and exposed concrete ceilings.

"The plan is kept as generic as possible so it can accept many futures, and the 'loose double skin' sustains a relationship with the surroundings that can stay open and diverse over a long time," Niko said.

"Life does not complete itself at the centre of the house but seeps out toward its edges. These in-between places have no proper names, but they are where people gather and time is well spent," he continued.

"This richness of the periphery is something an urban house cannot afford; in the countryside it is not needed, because a generous exterior is already there. Securing richness at the edge of the building itself is, to us, a very suburban act."

The rooftop living area of 100 Windows opens out onto a large terrace, which sits beneath an open grid of terracotta-toned concrete beams that is angled to continue the slope of the home's roof.

Other homes in Vietnam recently featured on Dezeen include an extension by ODDO Architects informed by Hanoi's narrow alleyways, and a home in Da Nang by Live Out Studio that is fronted by a perforated brick wall.

The photography is by Trieu Chien.

item.content:encoded:
Work has begun on the demolition of the never-opened Rike Concert Hall in Tbilisi, which was designed by Italian practice Studio Fuksas.

Local news organisation TV Pirveli filmed the cladding being removed from the Rike Concert Hall in central Tbilisi last week.

The work began less than two weeks after the Tbilisi city hall architecture department issued a permit allowing the building's owner to demolish the concert hall.

Designed by Studio Fuksas, the building in the central Rike Park has remained empty and closed since 2012, when it was largely complete.

The building was built as part of a rejuvenation plan for the city enacted under previous president Mikheil Saakashvili.

Georgia's change of government in 2012 is largely seen as the reason the project was abandoned, with the concert hall connected to the previous regime.

The extremely distinctive building consists of two tube-shaped volumes that open out onto the riverside park. Each of the tubes was covered in square stainless-steel panels that resemble scales.

In the news report published by TV Pirveli last week, a video was captured showing these cladding panels being removed and the structure underneath exposed.

Read:

Planned demolition of Tbilisi concert hall "a significant cultural setback" says Studio Fuksas

The demolition has begun less than 15 years after construction of the building's structure was largely complete, although the internal fit-out never happened.

After a decade of closure, the building was sold to a property developer in 2022, who in turn sold it to the current owner – Makro Constructions – in 2025.

Following news of the planned demolition last month, Studio Fuksas described the plans as "a significant cultural setback". In a statement to Dezeen, it claimed that the studio had received no response to efforts to contact the local government.

"Over the past months, the studio repeatedly offered to work with the Georgian authorities to explore alternative solutions that could preserve and repurpose this iconic building, avoiding what we believe would be a premature and irreversible demolition," said the studio.

"Unfortunately, these proposals have received no response."

The photography is courtesy of Studio Fuksas.

item.content:encoded:
Scottish architect Ruairidh Moir has launched a campaign to rebuild the fire-torn Mackintosh Building at the Glasgow School of Art, calling on "an independent body to own and take forward the project".

The campaign calls for the building's ownership to be transferred to an independent organisation to deliver a "faithful restoration and reinstatement". It also asks the Scottish and UK governments for financial assistance.

At the time of writing, it has 5,406 signatures. The target is 100,000, at which stage the petition will be "hand-delivered" to both Scottish and UK Governments and the board of Glasgow School of Art (GSA).

The campaign follows GSA's recent announcement that it cannot afford to rebuild the iconic Mackintosh Building, known affectionately as The Mack, without external funding.

Moir, a conservation architect and founder of Glasgow studio BARD, said he initiated the petition to "reflect the views of many people who have cared deeply about the school for years".

"We owe it to Charles Rennie Mackintosh"

"There has been frustration at the GSA's stewardship of the building, both before the fires and in the years that have followed," Moir told Dezeen.

"The recent statements by the School of Art governors have galvanised many to step forward and unite to remove the obstructions and demonstrate support for Mackintosh's masterpiece," he continued.

The fire-torn art school is the best-known building designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, Scotland's most famous architect.

A fire ripped through the building in 2014, before a second and more destructive fire occurred during a £35 million restoration project in 2018.

Shortly after the second blaze, the former director of the GSA Tom Inns said that it would be rebuilt. But restoration works are now on hold.

In Moir's view, it needs to be rebuilt as "it is genuinely one of the finest achievements of architecture".

"The Mack must be rebuilt because it is so important. Architecture of such renowned and recognised quality is not that common. This one sits amongst the very highest tier of architectural achievement and is beloved," he explained.

"We owe it to Charles Rennie Mackintosh, Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh, Fra Newbery, and to all those who have loved the building; to our culture and heritage; and to our sense of self, to get this right for Scotland and for the world."

GSA has "continually failed"

While the campaign calls for the ownership of the building to be transferred, it also states the building should be made available "on a lease-back arrangement to GSA" to make sure it can remain as an art school.

Moir added that a panel of experts would need to be created to advise a new design and project team.

"The need for an independent body to own and take forward the project, protecting it for future generations, is borne out by the fact that the GSA board has continually failed to deliver it," explained Moir.

"There is understandably little confidence in allowing the body that has failed Mackintosh's masterpiece in this way to have a third attempt. Time for a fresh start."

For Moir, the thought of the school being left as a ruin "leaves [him] cold".

While there is also always a risk of pastiche in reconstruction work, the architect believes it can be achieved to the same quality as the original.

Read:

Glasgow School of Art "cannot rebuild" Mackintosh Building

"There are huge challenges in achieving it, but the will, finance, client, leadership and skills all need to be there for a successful outcome," he said. "We cannot allow incompatible or phoney materials to be used; it must be authentic to the way Mackintosh left it for us to care for."

"Few buildings are as comprehensively recorded as the School of Art. Backing away from a full and faithful reinstatement because of loose arguments around pastiche or authenticity would, in my view, be a profound mistake. We have almost everything at our fingertips to faithfully reinstate the building."

Since GSA's announcement, many industry figures have spoken out with views similar to Moir. Among them was British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who compared the need to rebuild to Notre-Dame Cathedral.

"To accept a diminished future for it would show a worrying lack of cultural confidence," he wrote in an Instagram post shared by Humanise.

"When Notre-Dame burned, Paris didn't shrug and scale down its ambition. It responded with imagination, leadership and national will. Paris came out stronger afterwards," he said.

"Let's all urge the Scottish Government, Glasgow City Council, businesses, funders, cultural leaders and communities to work together with GSA to find a way to restore the Mackintosh Building with the care, seriousness and ambition it deserves."

item.title: "Plants on a building doesn't make it sustainable, any more than a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan"
item.dc:creator: Barnabas Calder
item.description:
Plans for a large new building in Rotterdam intended to encourage people to lead more environmentally friendly lifestyles are wrong-headed and should be scrapped in a blaze of publicity, writes Barnabas Calder. Putting plants on a building doesn't make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan. Yet

item.content:encoded:
Plans for a large new building in Rotterdam intended to encourage people to lead more environmentally friendly lifestyles are wrong-headed and should be scrapped in a blaze of publicity, writes Barnabas Calder.

Putting plants on a building doesn't make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan. Yet image searches for "sustainable architecture" puke out a page of gas-guzzling big new buildings with greenery on their walls or balconies.

Dutch architecture studio MVRDV has won a competition with a new specimen of plant-washing, the Shift Embassy. Let's hope it remains unbuilt.

The client, social enterprise Shift, declares that "a fossil-fuel-based economy built on the unsustainable myth of perpetual economic growth [is] leading us toward ecological and social catastrophe." True, and each summer the proof obtrudes itself in longer, hotter heatwaves, bigger wildfires and worsening crop failures.

I would be happy for it to look considerably worse if it were less harmful environmentally

The Shift Embassy, also called "Rotterdam Rocks!", is a bizarre response to the organisation's anti-growth stance: a 200-bed hotel, posh restaurant, offices, and a 5,000-square-metre exhibition space for attracting international tourists to Rotterdam, in the hope that once they are there they will think hard enough about sustainability to go home and change their lives.

Its aesthetics are attracting the usual derision that clusters round different-looking buildings – comparisons with the Flintstones, with faeces and with genitalia. The same practice's Marble Arch Mound showed how hard it can be to make urban vegetation schemes convincing.

Looks, though, seem a trivial concern in the face of ecological catastrophe. I would be happy for it to look considerably worse if it were less harmful environmentally.

Read:

MVRDV wins competition for "new world wonder" in the Netherlands

The "rock-like" surfaces of the architects' press release turn out, on some more clicking around, to be concrete. MVRDV promises "low-carbon concrete", but if that's a matter of swapping cement for industrial co-products such as GGBS the benefits for emissions may be negligible at best. As the Institution of Structural Engineers warns, the supply of GGBS is already almost at capacity, so trucking it in for this building likely means another project will miss out, and have to use normal higher-carbon cement instead.

The engineering relies on reclaimed steel. Reusing a beam is often better than melting it down, but again, if not reclaimed for this project the same steel would be either reclaimed or recycled for another project. Around 70 per cent of all steel still comes from ore, with recycling and reclamation already using most scrap steel. Reclaimed steel is, in other words, also no magic bullet for decarbonisation.

There are some good initiatives in the proposal. The exhibition area will be allowed a certain latitude of temperature variation across the year, as opposed to the offices, hotel and restaurant, which require "high-quality indoor environments" – code, presumably, for the uncomfortably excessive cooling of most commercial interiors in summer, and overbearing heating during winter.

The message given by the building as a whole is wrong

The restaurant will be plant-based. Shift also aims to grow as much greenery as it can around the building. If you really must build a new building, a wider temperature range, extensive planting and meat-free catering are good measures.

There is a welcome honesty to the way Shift discusses the downsides of an "iconic" new building. Its argument is that by influencing visitors' future behaviour, "the societal impact is estimated to be 10,000 times greater than the environmental impact associated with the building's construction and energy use".

This figure assumes that over 50 years, 20 per cent of 25,000,000 projected visitors will lastingly drop two tonnes per year from their personal carbon footprint as a result of the visit.

Read:

"It's time to see all those circular economy strategies for what they are"

But even if that figure proves robust, what about the societal impact of the architecture itself? Unfortunately, the more successfully Shift establishes itself in the minds of a wide international public as a leader in sustainability, the more harm its building can do.

Whatever nuanced analysis Shift conducts of the qualities and problems tied to experimenting with low-carbon materials, the message given by the building as a whole is wrong. It supports the myth that sustainable architecture means new, tall concrete and steel buildings with lifts and powerful air-treatment systems, but some plants on them.

Shift acknowledges that retrofitting an existing building would have been more sustainable, but says there was no suitable candidate in the big new Waterkant development its embassy will be part of. Instead, the organisation ran a major architecture competition for something new, dense and iconic – a brief that could only realistically be executed with profoundly unsustainable materials and methods, and that depends thereafter on millions of tourists flying round the world in environmentally destructive pursuit of distraction and novelty.

If Shift now abandons this project in a blaze of publicity it will do immense good

This is not the degrowth that Shift calls for, but it's not too late to fix things. If Shift now abandons this project in a blaze of publicity, explaining that the environmental cost is too high – an example of outdated and profoundly unsustainable architectural thinking – it will do immense good, and will demonstrate a profound and inspiring commitment to degrowth.

Should that lose the organisation some funding, so be it. Maximising income, investment and capital expenditure is not a degrowth approach.

Shift's own estimates of the good its building will do are based on pilot activities where it reports participants dropped their emissions by an average of 30 per cent. Why not spend the reported €240,000,000 that the building will cost delivering more of these remarkably effective pilot activities instead?

Read:

Can we quit our air-con addiction?

That would save the 15,000 tonnes of carbon-dioxide-equivalent emissions that it reports will be required to produce and power the MVRDV building over 50 years, and the 35,000,000 tonnes it assumes will be emitted as a result of people travelling there. More importantly, though, Shift could push back against architecture's devastating environmental harms by setting such a powerful, well-evidenced example of having the courage not to go ahead with an avoidable building project.

At present, the construction industry and the running of buildings together amount to 37 per cent of global carbon emissions. The most inspirational thing that any architecture practice or client can do is to radically opt out of this harm: make brilliant use of what's already here; tweak and improve in modest, impactful ways; spread the word about the immense ecological harms done by our making and running new buildings.

Shift has the chance to be the ambassador for a real shift – a shift to understanding that sustainable architecture means a new wooden shutter on an old window, not a big bulk of concrete, steel and HVAC peeping out guiltily from behind a leafy toupée.

Barnabas Calder is head of the History of Architecture Research Cluster at the University of Liverpool, and author of Architecture: From Prehistory To Climate Emergency (2021) and Raw Concrete: The Beauty of Brutalism (2016).

Exhibitions Architecture's Inscriptions, Maggie's: Architecture That Cares and Wellbeing in the City are among the architecture and design events featured in Dezeen Events Guide this August.

Other events taking place during the month include Helsinki Design Week, Jia Curated and The Art-Marotte Masterclass Series.

Maggie's: Architecture That Cares
6 March to 1 November, UK

Presented at the V&A Dundee, Maggie's: Architecture That Cares is an exhibition celebrating the architecture behind UK-based charity Maggie's.

The exhibition features models of the cancer care centres, including work by architects Norman Foster, Frank Gehry, Zaha Hadid,  Richard Rogers and Benedetta Tagliabue.

Wellbeing in the City
24 April to 20 September, Spain

The Wellbeing in the City exhibition explores how traditional architecture has impacted the biological, social and spatial experiences of people living in urban spaces.

The display outlines eight key elements of impact, including birth, nurturing, eating, healing, sleeping, playing, courting and walking.

The showcase is curated by architecture practice Izaskun Chinchilla and takes place at La Arquería de Nuevos Ministerios in Madrid.

Architecture's Inscriptions
9 July to 7 October, China

This exhibition demonstrates the influence ancient manuscripts, calligraphy, scholar's rocks, paintings and rubbings have on the work of contemporary Chinese architects.

Architects Huang Wenjing, Li Hu, Liu Jiakun, Liu Yichun, Zhang Ke, Zhu Xiaofeng and Zhuang Shen and artists Ding Yi, Xu Bing and Zhan Wang are all taking part in Architecture's Inscriptions, which takes place at Tank Shanghai.

Jia Curated
13 to 17 August, Indonesia

Jia Curated is an annual design, craft and culture festival taking place in Bali, welcoming over 250 brands across the fields of art, architecture, materiality, landscape design and construction.

This year's event will follow the theme Nature Weave, addressing "interwoven relationships" between people and nature, and the impact on design and craft, such as biophilia practices.

The Art-Marotte Masterclass Series
17 to 21 August, Belgium

A five-day workshop programme will take place at Château Art-Marotte in Braives, Belgium, inviting postgraduate students to experiment with ceramics and materiality.

The masterclass series will offer students the experience to develop their skills in ceramic screen printing and sculpture, using materials such as slumped glass and plaster.

Helsinki Design Week
28 August to 6 September, Finland

Helsinki Design Week celebrates its 21st anniversary in August with the theme The Oncoming Other, spotlighting community, collaboration and connection in urban space.

The programme of exhibitions, talks and open showrooms explores a range of disciplines, including textile, product, industrial, fashion, interior and graphic design.

About Dezeen Events Guide

Dezeen Events Guide is our guide to the best architecture and design events taking place across the world each year. The guide is updated weekly and includes virtual events, conferences, trade fairs, major exhibitions and design weeks.

Inclusion in the guide is free for basic listings, with events selected at Dezeen's discretion. Organisers can get standard, enhanced or featured listings for their events, including images, additional text and links, by paying a modest fee.

In addition, events can ensure inclusion by partnering with Dezeen. For more details on inclusion in Dezeen Events Guide and media partnerships with Dezeen, email eventsguide@dezeen.com.

item.content:encoded:
The UK government has announced the arrival of plug-in solar panels that can be fitted onto balconies to reduce household energy costs.

Expected to be sold in UK stores before the end of summer, the low-cost panels, which are already widely used across Europe, connect directly to a mains socket and can be placed on balconies, roofs or any outdoor space without installation.

Following an announcement by the government in March, recent changes to existing plug and electricity safety regulations in the UK will allow the use of these plug-in solar devices from 27th August.

The new legislation means that UK households, including flat owners and renters, will be able to generate their own electricity and cut energy bills.

New legislation "a major win" for UK households

"Seeing these systems available in stores by summer would be a major win for households, enabling people to take advantage of the longer, brighter days and start generating their own clean electricity straight away," head of UK communications for EcoFlow Lorna Wallace-Smith said.

"For many households – particularly those living in flats or rented homes – solar has not always been straightforward. Plug-and-play systems remove that barrier, making it far easier to get started," Wallace-Smith added.

Read:

New homes in England to have bird-friendly swift bricks in planning reform

The move, which was published under the Starmer Labour government, is part of a wider clean energy initiative that aims to reduce the UK's dependency on global fossil fuel markets as energy costs soar amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Solar panels to become standard for new homes

Alongside the legislation, new rules for the Future Homes Standard are set to come into force next March, mandating low-carbon heating and on-site solar panels for the majority of new homes.

According to the government, these new measures could reportedly save households up to £830 a year on energy bills, as well as create 75 per cent less carbon emissions than homes built to the 2013 standards.

"The Future Homes Standard is a landmark moment for clean energy in Britain," Energy UK's chief executive Dhara Vyas said.

"New homes built under this standard will benefit from clean heating solutions and solar, protecting households from volatile gas prices and putting energy security within the home itself," Vyas added.

Other recent sustainability initiatives in the UK include policy changes to the National Planning Policy Framework requiring new builds to be fitted with bird-friendly swift bricks.

Meanwhile, in the US, the American Institute of Architects has "celebrated" a recently passed bill aimed at speeding up the building and access of affordable housing in the country.
